He was made Military Governor of Fu Prefecture, then shifted to garrison command of Cao and Zhen; soon afterward he governed Lu Prefecture, where the people asked that he stay three more years and received an imperial commendation.

He was made Observation Commissioner of Fu Prefecture, then shifted to garrison command of Chan and Zhen; soon afterward he governed Lu Prefecture, where the people asked that he stay three more years and an edict commended him.
涪州觀察使 is Observation Commissioner of Fu, and 澶 is Chan, not Cao; 詔獎之 is an edict commending him.

He was changed to Military Governor of Fu Prefecture, transferred to garrison deployment of Cao and Zhen prefectures; soon he was made prefect of Lu; the people begged to keep him three years; an edict commended him.

He was changed to Observation Commissioner of Fu Prefecture, transferred to garrison deployment of Chan and Zhen prefectures; soon he was made prefect of Lu; the people begged to keep him three years; an edict commended him.
The literal line has the same errors: 觀察使 is not Military Governor, and 澶州 is Chan, not Cao.

He lost his father when he was only a few years old and was raised by his uncle Qian, a junior officer in the Bureau of Armaments; later he followed his mother into Wei Renpu's household. The imperial son-in-law Xianxin was his half-brother on his mother's side.

He lost his father when he was only a few years old and was raised by his uncle Qian, a vice director in the Bureau of Operations; later he followed his mother into Wei Renpu's household. The imperial son-in-law Xianxin was his half-brother on his mother's side.
職方員外郎 is a vice director in the Bureau of Operations, not a junior officer of a Bureau of Armaments.

At several sui he lost his father and was raised by his uncle, Director of the Bureau of Armaments Qian; later he followed his mother to the household of Wei Renpu; the emperor's son-in-law Xianxin was his maternal half-brother.

At several sui he lost his father and was raised by his uncle, Vice Director of the Bureau of Operations Qian; later he followed his mother to the household of Wei Renpu; the emperor's son-in-law Xianxin was his maternal half-brother.
員外郎 is vice director and 職方 is the Bureau of Operations, not director of a Bureau of Armaments.

Coastal merchants then sailed to trade in foreign goods, while Java, Srivijaya, Parhae, Champa, and other lands also sent annual missions to court, so that rhinoceros horn, ivory, aromatics, medicinals, and other rarities overflowed the storehouses.

Coastal merchants then sailed to trade in foreign goods, while Java, Srivijaya, Boni, Champa, and other lands also sent annual missions to court, so that rhinoceros horn, ivory, aromatics, medicinals, and other rarities overflowed the storehouses.
渤泥 is Boni, a maritime tribute state; Parhae would be 渤海, a different polity.

Merchants along the coast then sailed to trade foreign goods; Java, Srivijaya, Parhae, Zhan City and other states also came annually to court; thus rhinoceros, elephant, incense, medicines and rare goods filled the treasuries.

Merchants along the coast then sailed to trade foreign goods; Java, Srivijaya, Boni, Champa and other states also came annually to court; thus rhinoceros, elephant, incense, medicines and rare goods filled the treasuries.
渤泥 is Boni, not Parhae, and 占城 is Champa, not a calque 'Zhan City'.
One day Xun and others returned late to private quarters; Zhun was side by side with Wen Zhongshu in bridles, and a mad commoner met their horses and bowed shouting "Long live!"
One day Xun and others returned late to private quarters; Zhun was riding abreast with Wen Zhongshu, and a mad commoner met their horses and bowed shouting "Long live!"
並轡 means riding abreast; 'in bridles' is a false calque that obscures the scene.

His son Minzhong was first made an Attendant Official; while Xun served at the Palace Directorate, Minzhong petitioned that he had studied letters and wished to change rank, and was at once transferred to assistant director in the Court of Judicial Review, rising in time to department director in the Ministry of Revenue.

His son Minzhong was first made an Attendant Official; while Xun served at the Palace Directorate, Xun memorialized that Minzhong had studied letters and wished to change rank, and Minzhong was at once transferred to assistant director in the Court of Judicial Review, rising in time to department director in the Ministry of Revenue.
遜在宣徽，表言 names Xun as the memorialist; Minzhong is the son whose literary study is reported, not the petitioner.

Son Minzhong was first appointed Attendant Official; while Xun was at the Palace Directorate, he memorialized that he had once studied literature and wished to change rank; he was immediately exchanged to Assistant Director of the Court of Judicial Review, accumulating to Department Head in the Ministry of Public Works.

Son Minzhong was first appointed Attendant Official; while Xun was at the Palace Directorate, Xun memorialized that Minzhong had studied literature and wished to change rank; Minzhong was immediately transferred to Assistant Director of the Court of Judicial Review, later reaching Department Director of the Bureau of Review (Ministry of Revenue).
Collapsed pronouns hide that Xun memorialized for Minzhong, and 比部郎中 is Bureau of Review under Revenue, not Public Works.
His original name was Rong; Taizong changed the written form of his name to one signifying smelting ore and said, "It is through firing clay in a kiln that vessels are formed."
His original name was Rong; Taizong changed the written form of his name to one signifying smelting ore and said, "It is by molding and smelting that vessels are formed."
陶鎔所以成器也 is a molding-and-smelting metaphor for the rename to 鎔; the kiln-clay quote is wrong, but the proposed English inserts Chinese characters.
He was the son of Right Royal Guard Senior General Zhou Jing.
He was the son of Right Leading Army Guard Senior General Zhou Jing.
右領軍衛 is the Leading Army Guard, not a Royal Guard, but the original's Zhou Jing correctly identifies 景 from the Zhou Ying biography and should be kept.

Tianxiong Military Commissioner Sun Yongyou and Transport Commissioner Yang Chen praised him; he was also sent to inspect border affairs in Sui and Yin prefectures, and on his return his memorial pleased the emperor and he was promoted to Deputy Commissioner of the Saddle and Bridle Repository.

Tianxiong Military Commissioner Sun Yongyou and Transport Commissioner Yang Jian praised him; he was also sent to inspect border affairs in Sui and Yin prefectures, and on his return his memorial pleased the emperor and he was promoted to Deputy Commissioner of the Saddle and Bridle Repository.
楊緘 is Yang Jian; Chen does not match 緘.
When Zhenzong succeeded to the throne, Chenggui was separately sent to Hebei to proclaim the news, and Ying was additionally given concurrent prefect of Fuyang.
When Zhenzong succeeded to the throne, Chenggui was separately sent to Hebei to proclaim the news, and Ying was additionally given concurrent prefect of Fu Prefecture.
加領富州刺史 is a concurrent prefecture of Fu, not the city name Fuyang.
The emperor judged Ying mediocre, timid, and dull, replaced him with Cao Wei, and transferred him to govern Cao Prefecture.
The emperor judged Ying mediocre, timid, and dull, replaced him with Cao Wei, and transferred him to govern Chan Prefecture.
徙知澶州 is Chan Prefecture (Chanyuan), not 曹州 Cao.
The emperor said Ying was mediocre, cowardly and unwise; Cao Wei replaced him; he was transferred to know Cao Prefecture.
The emperor said Ying was mediocre, cowardly and unwise; Cao Wei replaced him; he was transferred to know Chan Prefecture.
The literal likewise misreads 澶州 as Cao Prefecture.

The transport commissioner reported his negligence, so he was moved to Cao Prefecture, where bandits repeatedly appeared within the borders; the councilors, noting that he held a commander's post yet could not quiet the region by prestige, asked that he be shifted elsewhere.

The transport commissioner reported his negligence, so he was moved to Chan Prefecture, where bandits repeatedly appeared within the borders; the councilors, noting that he held a commander's post yet could not quiet the region by prestige, asked that he be shifted elsewhere.
徙知澶州 after the Zhen-Ding posting is again Chan, not Cao.

The transport commissioner memorialized his laxness; he was transferred to know Cao Prefecture; within the territory bandits repeatedly appeared; the grand councilors, because Ying held a general's post, could not calm by prestige, and requested moving him to another prefecture.

The transport commissioner memorialized his laxness; he was transferred to know Chan Prefecture; within the territory bandits repeatedly appeared; the grand councilors, because Ying held a general's post, could not calm by prestige, and requested moving him to another prefecture.
The literal must render 澶州 as Chan Prefecture, not Cao.
Because Chanyuan lay on the Khitan line of attack and its generous grain stipends were hard to give up, he was again appointed to govern Cao Prefecture.
Because Chanyuan lay on the Khitan line of attack and its generous grain stipends were hard to give up, he was again appointed to govern Chan Prefecture.
復命知澶州 restates the same Chan/Chanyuan posting already named 澶淵 in the sentence, not Cao.
Also because Chanyuan faced the Khitan thrust, relying on its generous grain stipends, he was again ordered to know Cao Prefecture.
Also because Chanyuan faced the Khitan thrust, relying on its generous grain stipends, he was again ordered to know Chan Prefecture.
The literal's Cao Prefecture contradicts 澶州 / 澶淵 in the same unit.
Soon he served as military commissioner of Cao Prefecture.
Soon he served as controller-general of Chan Prefecture.
澶州鈐轄 is controller-general of Chan Prefecture, not military commissioner of Cao.
Soon he filled the post of military commissioner of Cao Prefecture.
Soon he filled the post of Chan Prefecture controller-general.
鈐轄 is controller-general and the prefecture is 澶州 Chan, not Cao.
When the emperor went to Cao Prefecture and the Khitan sought peace, Jiying took part in the strategic consultations.
When the emperor went to Chan Prefecture and the Khitan sought peace, Jiying took part in the strategic consultations.
從幸澶州 is the Chanyuan peace site Chan Prefecture, not Cao.
Following the emperor to Cao Prefecture, when the Khitan requested peace and strategy was consulted, Jiying participated.
Following the emperor to Chan Prefecture, when the Khitan requested peace and strategy was consulted, Jiying participated.
The literal must follow the emperor to Chan Prefecture, 澶州, not Cao.
That summer, by regulation he was appointed Military Affairs Commissioner.
That summer, by edict he was appointed Military Affairs Commissioner.
制授 is appointment by imperial edict (制), not 'by regulation'.

While Xia and Yibu were troubled by raids, Xian memorialized, "In recent years the frontier has not been quiet: Li Jiqian has turned ungrateful in Ling and Xia, Wang Xiaobo has rebelled in Ba and Qiong, and armies have been raised both in Hexi and in the southwest.

While Xia Terrace and Yibu were troubled by raids, Xian memorialized, "In recent years the frontier has not been quiet: Li Jiqian has turned ungrateful in Ling and Xia, Wang Xiaobo has rebelled in Ba and Qiong, and armies have been raised both in Hexi and in the southwest.
夏臺 is the toponym Xia Terrace, distinct from 靈、夏 later in the memorial.

Rain had been falling steadily, and the Khitan bowstrings of leather had gone slack and useless in the wet; Xian therefore inflicted a great defeat, captured fifteen named princes and noble generals along with two Imperial Guard seal knobs, and took twenty thousand heads.

Rain had been falling steadily, and the Khitan bowstrings of leather had gone slack and useless in the wet; Xian therefore inflicted a great defeat, killing or capturing fifteen named princes and noble generals along with two Imperial Guard seal knobs, and took twenty thousand heads.
梟獲 is more than 'captured', but 'beheaded and captured' makes the fifteen notables both killed and taken alive; the tally is killing or capturing them.

Otherwise send one thousand cavalry and three thousand infantry to cross the river at Pu Prefecture, sweep across Cao Prefecture, then follow with the great army pursuing north in concealed strike—this too can catch them unawares."

Otherwise send one thousand cavalry and three thousand infantry to cross the river at Pu Prefecture, sweep across Chan Prefecture, then follow with the great army pursuing north in concealed strike—this too can catch them unawares."
橫掠澶州 is Chan Prefecture; the literal's Cao is a mistranslation of 澶, not a variant 澽.

At the time the imperial carriage was ascending the mausoleum; Xian told his guests and aides: "My remaining years and rank have reached the extreme; today the Son of Heaven's road passes through Hulao—I cannot once bow to the dust of the attendant carriage; this is a remaining regret!"

At the time the imperial carriage was ascending the mausoleum; Xian told his guests and aides: "My years and rank have reached the extreme; today the Son of Heaven's road passes through Hulao—I cannot once bow to the dust of the attendant carriage; this is a remaining regret!"
余 is the speaker's 'I'; 余年位偕極 is 'my years and rank have both reached their height', not remaining years.
